strings.name: Roberta Metsola
strings.role: President of the European Parliament and Maltese Nationalist Party politician
strings.summary: Roberta Metsola is a Maltese lawyer and politician who entered the European Parliament in 2013, became its president in 2022 and was re-elected in 2024. Her work spans European law, border governance, parliamentary transparency and support for Ukraine. The presidency entails chairing proceedings and representing Parliament, not leading the European Commission or European Council; collective legislative outcomes cannot all be credited to one person.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through 18 November 2026. The 2024 presidential election conferred a two-and-a-half-year term until 2027; calls for a future term are not completed elections. Recent activity is supported by published official addresses of 9 and 11 November, rather than schedules alone.
strings.influence.rationale: Chairs the European Parliament in its legislative, budgetary and representative work, with influence on transnational democratic governance and European policy coordination.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and legal education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 18 January 1979 in St Julians, Malta, she graduated from the University of Malta and the College of Europe in Bruges, specialising in European law and politics. As a student she campaigned for Malta’s EU membership and served as secretary-general of European Democrat Students in 2002–2003.
strings.facts.f2.label: Party and parliamentary affiliation
strings.facts.f2.value: A member of Malta’s Nationalist Party, she sits with the European People’s Party Group. After filling a vacant seat in 2013, she was re-elected in 2014, 2019 and 2024. She remains an MEP while serving as president.
strings.highlights.h1.title: The presidency’s institutional role
strings.highlights.h1.text: MEPs elect the president to preside over parliamentary proceedings and represent Parliament in dealings with other institutions. The normally renewable two-and-a-half-year presidency differs from the five-year legislative term; legislation, budgets and oversight remain collective institutional and parliamentary work.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Parliamentary activity in November 2026
strings.highlights.h2.text: On 9 November she called for stronger multilateral cooperation at the opening of the OACPS–EU Joint Parliamentary Assembly. On 11 November she opened the Brussels plenary by commemorating Armistice Day and victims of war. Published addresses record completed events; cooperation goals are not accomplished policy results.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Re-elected president of the European Parliament
strings.timeline.t1.text: She received 562 votes in the first presidential ballot of the tenth Parliament. There were 699 ballots, including 76 blank or invalid ones. Her new term covers the first two and a half years, until 2027, rather than automatically the full five-year legislature.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Outlines integrity reforms to Parliament
strings.timeline.t2.text: Following a crisis of trust prompted by a corruption investigation, she outlined stronger lobbying and financial disclosures, rules on former members’ conflicts of interest and whistleblowing training. The statement described initial agreement and proposed steps, not proof that every reform was in force or corruption eliminated.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Visits Kyiv and addresses Ukraine’s parliament
strings.timeline.t3.text: After Russia’s full-scale invasion, she visited Kyiv and met Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Denys Shmyhal and Ruslan Stefanchuk to express support. The next day she visited a school in Poland receiving people fleeing the war. Diplomatic solidarity is distinguished from actual funding or equipment delivery.
strings.timeline.t4.title: First elected president of the European Parliament
strings.timeline.t4.text: She won 458 votes in the first round to serve the second half of the ninth Parliament. She had already acted as president after David Sassoli died on 11 January; the election and start of acting duties are separate. She became the third woman president and the youngest person elected to the post at that time.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Elected first vice-president
strings.timeline.t5.text: She replaced Mairead McGuinness, who had become a European commissioner. As the only candidate by the nomination deadline, she was declared elected by the president; no competitive ballot tally is invented.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Participates in border and coast guard reform talks
strings.timeline.t6.text: As Parliament’s rapporteur on Frontex reform, she participated in negotiations whose parliamentary and Council representatives reached a provisional agreement that day. It envisaged a 10,000-person standing corps by 2027 with rights and data safeguards. Formal approval was still required; 10,000 was a target, not staff already deployed that day.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Enters Parliament through a vacancy election
strings.timeline.t7.text: She was elected as a Nationalist candidate in the casual-election procedure to fill Simon Busuttil’s vacated seat. Three women won seats that day, so she is not described as Malta’s sole first female MEP.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Becomes Catherine Ashton’s legal adviser
strings.timeline.t8.text: After working on legal, judicial and home affairs at Malta’s Permanent Representation to the EU from 2004 to 2012, she joined EU foreign-policy High Representative Catherine Ashton’s team as legal adviser until 2013. She was not herself the High Representative.
